title: EMD-Corr for Explainable Retinal Classification
paper: Evaluation of EMD-Corr for Explainable Retinal Image Classification
summary: Evaluating patch-based explanations across fundus and OCT images, with Discriminative Patch Weighting and systematic ablation studies.
metricNote: Best reported configuration; a separate fundus evaluation reached 52.07%.
progress: From inspecting existing explanations to adapting and developing patch-based explanation methods.
overview: Can a patch-based explanation framework transfer across retinal imaging modalities? This study evaluates EMD-Corr, which uses Earth Mover’s Distance and patch-level re-ranking, on fundus and OCT images. It examines classification performance alongside the visual correspondences supporting predictions.
role: Adapted and evaluated EMD-Corr across two ophthalmic imaging modalities.
Developed Discriminative Patch Weighting (DPW) using Fisher Discriminative Scores to weight discriminative patch features.
Conducted ablation experiments covering domain adaptation, classifier choice, preprocessing, patch-grid resolution, and DPW.
data: EyePACS fundus subset: 3,568 images covering five diabetic retinopathy classes.
OCT2017 subset: 3,200 images across CNV, DME, Drusen, and Normal.
approach: Compared ResNet50 softmax classification, k-nearest neighbors using 2,048-dimensional global average-pooled features, and EMD-Corr using spatial features from layer4.
Compared 7 × 7 and 14 × 14 patch grids and evaluated the DPW strategy.
Examined how domain-specific fine-tuning affects classification and patch matching.
results: Domain adaptation substantially improved performance in both modalities. Patch correspondences provided visual evidence that could be examined alongside predictions. The best reported values come from the study’s configuration experiments; they are not comparisons against the other portfolio projects.
limitations: Expert lesion annotations were unavailable, so the clinical correctness of patch localization could not be quantitatively established.
Visual correspondences alone do not establish explanation faithfulness or clinical reliability.
next: Investigate expert-annotated Vietnamese retinal datasets and clinician evaluation of explanation usefulness.

title: AMD Diagnosis from OCT Images
paper: Performance Evaluation and Explainability Assessment of Deep Learning Architectures for AMD Diagnosis in OCT Images
summary: Comparing CNN, attention-enhanced CNN, and transformer models through cross-validation and visual explanations.
progress: Extending evaluation to stability and explanation behavior, beyond predictive scores alone.
overview: This study compares architectures for classifying OCT images into CNV, Drusen, and Normal. It examines predictive performance, stability across folds, and the image regions emphasized by visual explanations.
role: Evaluated ResNet50, ResNet50 with CBAM, and Swin Transformer-Tiny under a shared experimental setup.
Applied three-fold cross-validation to assess performance variability.
Investigated how CBAM affected Grad-CAM localization and background distraction.
data: A balanced subset of 3,000 images from the Mendeley OCT Dataset, with 1,000 images per class.
Images were resized to 224 × 224 pixels, converted to RGB, and normalized using ImageNet statistics.
No augmentation was used in the baseline experiments.
approach: Used two-stage transfer learning: five epochs with the backbone frozen, followed by 15 fine-tuning epochs.
Compared a conventional CNN, channel and spatial attention through CBAM, and a vision transformer.
Examined model behavior using Grad-CAM and attention maps.
results: ResNet50 achieved the strongest overall predictive performance. The CBAM model achieved the highest reported CNV recall and lower accuracy variability across folds. More localized visualizations were examined as qualitative evidence, not proof of clinical reliability.
limitations: The dataset was relatively small at 3,000 images.
Grad-CAM remains a post-hoc analysis tool. More localized heatmaps do not, by themselves, establish faithful explanations or clinical reliability.
next: Explore intrinsically interpretable, prototype-based architectures whose visual evidence is more closely connected to prediction.

title: Brain Tumor MRI: Beyond Accuracy
paper: Beyond Accuracy: Comparison of ResNet50 and GWN-Enhanced Models for Brain Tumor MRI Classification with LIME
summary: Investigating background reliance, shortcut learning, and the risks of slice-level evaluation behind near-perfect scores.
metricNote: Patient-wise separation could not be established.
progress: Asking what supports a prediction and whether the evaluation can be trusted.
overview: Does very high classification accuracy reflect reliable learning? This project compares models for No Tumor, Glioma, and Pituitary Tumor classification while examining background reliance and the risks associated with slice-level dataset splitting.
role: Compared standard ResNet50 with a Ghost Weight Normalization (GWN) variant.
Evaluated convergence speed and training stability.
Applied LIME to inspect image regions influencing predictions and examined how missing patient identifiers limit evaluation confidence.
data: A balanced subset of 3,300 images from a public Kaggle Brain Tumor MRI Dataset, with 1,100 images per class.
Training / validation / test: 80/10/10, corresponding to 2,640 / 330 / 330 images.
Images were resized to 224 × 224 pixels, converted to RGB, and normalized using ImageNet statistics. Augmentation included horizontal flipping and rotation up to 15°.
approach: Used five epochs of frozen-backbone training followed by up to 30 fine-tuning epochs.
Compared convergence and loss behavior between the baseline and GWN-enhanced model.
Used Local Interpretable Model-Agnostic Explanations (LIME) to investigate potential shortcut learning.
results: LIME revealed background reliance in both models, raising concerns about shortcut learning and evaluation validity. These scores do not establish generalization to unseen patients. LIME alone does not prove data leakage; it identifies behavior requiring further investigation.
limitations: Patient-wise separation could not be established because patient identifiers were unavailable.
The models were not evaluated on independent MRI data from Vietnamese hospitals.
next: Prioritize patient-level splitting, standardized Vietnamese hospital datasets, and out-of-distribution evaluation.

title: Diabetic Retinopathy Classification
paper: Study of Deep Learning Models for Diabetic Retinopathy Diagnosis
summary: Comparing three-class screening and five-class severity grading, with a focus on preprocessing and class imbalance.
progress: Building the foundation in preprocessing, transfer learning, class imbalance, and evaluation.
overview: This project compares three-class screening and five-class ICDRS severity classification from fundus images, with particular attention to preprocessing and class imbalance.
role: Designed a preprocessing pipeline combining black-border removal and CLAHE contrast enhancement.
Implemented class-balancing strategies using random oversampling, on-the-fly augmentation, and class weighting.
Compared ResNet50 and DenseNet121 across two classification settings and analyzed sensitivity alongside overall accuracy.
data: Training / validation / test: approximately 70/10/20, corresponding to 2,562 / 367 / 733 images.
approach: Removed black borders, applied CLAHE, resized images to 224 × 224 pixels, and normalized inputs.
Used random oversampling, a class weight of 1.5 for severe cases, and augmentation including rotation, zoom, brightness adjustment, and flipping.
Compared ResNet50 and DenseNet121 with global average pooling, dropout of 0.5, and a softmax head. Training used Adam with two warm-up epochs and up to 50 fine-tuning epochs.
results: DenseNet121 outperformed ResNet50 within the study’s experimental setup. For comparison, ResNet50 achieved 0.91 accuracy and 0.95 macro AUC in the three-class task, and 0.88 accuracy and 0.91 macro AUC in the five-class task.
limitations: Five-class sensitivity remained limited at 0.68, particularly where severity boundaries were subtle.
Patient clinical information was not incorporated; cross-validation and Grad-CAM were not included.
next: Explore multimodal approaches combining fundus images with clinical information such as patient age and diabetes duration.
